rationales.would: Would have reached presents reaching as the expected result, stronger than the chance specified.
rationales.might: Might have reached presents success as possible under the unreal condition, without guaranteeing it.
rationales.must: Must have reached makes a strong inference about a past result, not this uncertain alternative.
rationales.will: Will have reached expresses a confident completion or inference, not the uncertain unreal result.

findings: Compliance-review sentence repeated could still finish with inadequate context and feedback.
audit.microSkill: Might have for an uncertain counterfactual result
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes a possible imagined result from an expected one.
audit.levelReason: An unreal past alternative plus calibrated certainty is suitable B2 interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: Tentative counterfactual pairs conceptually with item 1988's confident outcome.

items.setupText: Choose the sentence expressing regret about not asking for a written quotation before the repair.
items.taskText: The bill is much higher than you expected.
options: I must have asked for a quotation.
I ought to have asked for a quotation.
I may have asked for a quotation.
I used to ask for a quotation.
items.answer: I ought to have asked for a quotation.
items.explanation: Ought to have + past participle expresses what would have been advisable before the past event.

This concludes that you did ask, contrary to the stated omission.
This leaves whether you asked uncertain, rather than evaluating the known omission.
Ought to have + past participle expresses what would have been advisable before the past event.
This describes a former habit rather than regret about this repair.

findings: Luis file-loss item differed from earlier items only in the person's name.
audit.microSkill: Ought to have for retrospective regret
audit.pedagogicalValue: Extends ought to to a missed past action using the perfect form.
audit.levelReason: Reflecting on a known omission and its consequence fits B2.
audit.similarityNote: First-person regret with ought to differs from third-person criticism with should.

items.setupText: The technician is reasonably optimistic but has not guaranteed success. Choose the meaning of the combined modal phrase.
items.taskText: 'With the replacement part, we should be able to restore the signal.'
options: The technician says that using the part is a compulsory repair step.
The technician concludes that the signal has already been restored.
The technician expects the part to make restoring the signal possible.
The technician gives the team permission to restore the signal.
items.answer: The technician expects the part to make restoring the signal possible.
items.explanation: Should expresses an expectation, while be able to concerns capability; together they predict that restoration will be possible.

rationales.The technician expects the part to make: Should expresses an expectation, while be able to concerns capability; together they predict that restoration will be possible.
rationales.The technician says that using the part: The comment expresses expected capability, not an instruction making a particular step compulsory.
rationales.The technician concludes that the signal: Be able to restore concerns capability for a coming action, not completed restoration.
rationales.The technician gives the team permission: The technician is estimating what the repair can achieve, not granting authorization.

findings: Training-office item was another closed-office deduction with generic feedback.
audit.microSkill: Should be able to for expected capability
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates expectation, ability, obligation, and actual achievement.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting two modal meanings in combination supports a B2 decision.
audit.similarityNote: Expected capability differs from a basic future-ability form question.

items.setupText: The speaker is confident that packing will finish before the collection time. Choose the completion expressing this future completion.
items.taskText: By the time the van arrives tomorrow, we ___ all the boxes.
items.explanation: Will have + past participle locates completion before a specified future point.

rationales.would have packed: Would have packed suggests an unreal or reported perspective, not this direct confident future prediction.
rationales.must have packed: Must have packed normally draws an inference about completed packing rather than locating a future completion as requested.
rationales.might have packed: Might have packed leaves completion uncertain, weaker than the stated confidence.
rationales.will have packed: Will have + past participle locates completion before a specified future point.

findings: Misunderstanding item repeated an unclear-answer frame with an unrelated compliance-check tail.
audit.microSkill: Will have for future completion
audit.pedagogicalValue: Relates completed action to a later future event.
audit.levelReason: Two future time points require B2 control of the perfect form.
audit.similarityNote: Future completion differs from by now expectations and past inference.

items.setupText: The assistant did disclose the password. You want to criticize that action, not guess whether it happened.
items.taskText: She ___ the password in a public chat.
items.explanation: Shouldn't have posted evaluates the completed action as inappropriate.

rationales.can't have posted: This denies the possibility of the posting, but the context confirms it happened.
rationales.shouldn't have posted: Shouldn't have posted evaluates the completed action as inappropriate.
rationales.might not have posted: This expresses uncertainty about non-posting, not criticism of the known action.
rationales.didn't have to post: This says posting was unnecessary, which does not directly express the requested criticism.

findings: Evaluation-memo badge item was another near-identical need-not sentence.
audit.microSkill: Shouldn't have for criticism of a completed action
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates disapproval of an event from denial that it happened.
audit.levelReason: A known past mistake supports B2 evaluation with a negative perfect modal.
audit.similarityNote: Criticizes an action taken, whereas item 1987 criticizes an omission.

items.setupText: The deadline requires the report to be finished before Monday's meeting. Choose the completion that explicitly expresses completion by that point.
items.taskText: We need ___ the report by the time the meeting begins.
items.explanation: Need to have + past participle makes completion before the stated point explicit.

rationales.to have finishing: The perfect construction takes finished, not finishing, after have.
rationales.have finished: Ordinary positive need requires to before the following verb phrase.
rationales.to have finished: Need to have + past participle makes completion before the stated point explicit.
rationales.to having finished: After need to, use the basic form have, not having.

findings: Technical-review sentence repeated the same could-versus-must ambiguity and boilerplate feedback.
audit.microSkill: Need to have done for completion by a deadline
audit.pedagogicalValue: Expresses a requirement concerning a completed state at a future time.
audit.levelReason: Combining necessity with a perfect infinitive is a meaningful upper-B2 demand.
audit.similarityNote: Required completion differs from the prediction in item 1998.

items.setupText: The editor expresses a preference about the researcher's future action. Choose the completion that preserves that future reference and uses the standard would-rather pattern.
items.taskText: I'd rather you ___ the results until we have checked the calculations.
items.explanation: With a different subject after would rather, a past form can express a present or future preference.

rationales.hadn't announced: The past perfect would express a preference about an earlier announcement, not the future action specified.
rationales.didn't announce: With a different subject after would rather, a past form can express a present or future preference.
rationales.didn't announced: Did already carries the past form; use announce, not announced, after didn't.
rationales.not to announce: After I'd rather you, use a finite clause such as you didn't announce, not a to-infinitive.

findings: Mina report preference was labelled an instruction and tested only basic would rather selection.
audit.microSkill: Would rather with another subject and future reference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates grammatical past form from actual past time in a preference clause.
audit.levelReason: Subject change and non-past meaning of a past form create a C1 distinction.
audit.similarityNote: Other-person future preference differs from own-action preference at B1.

items.setupText: Asked what the sponsors' withdrawal means for next month's festival, an analyst gives this response. Choose the closest meaning of may well.
items.taskText: 'With two major sponsors withdrawing, the festival may well be cancelled.'
options: Cancellation is the action the analyst recommends.
Cancellation has been formally authorized by the sponsors.
Cancellation is a credible, perhaps likely outcome.
Cancellation is an established fact that the analyst concedes.
items.answer: Cancellation is a credible, perhaps likely outcome.
items.explanation: May well presents an outcome as quite possible or unsurprising given the circumstances, without making it certain.

rationales.Cancellation is the action the analyst r: The context is prediction; may well does not state what organizers ought to do.
rationales.Cancellation has been formally authorize: This sentence does not use may to grant permission or report authorization.
rationales.Cancellation is a credible, perhaps like: May well presents an outcome as quite possible or unsurprising given the circumstances, without making it certain.
rationales.Cancellation is an established fact that: The analyst is estimating what may happen, not acknowledging a known cancellation.

findings: Committee may-well item admitted other coherent modals and falsely framed the prediction as a requirement.
audit.microSkill: May well for a supported possibility
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes strengthened possibility from advice, permission, and concession.
audit.levelReason: The stance conveyed by well and the excluded modal readings suit C1.
audit.similarityNote: Predictive may well contrasts with acknowledged-fact may in item 2007.

items.setupText: Read the cautious planning statement. Choose what is and is not settled.
items.taskText: 'If the venue loses its licence, we might have to relocate the conference.'
options: The licence will be lost, making relocation necessary.
The organizers prefer relocation if the licence is lost.
Relocation could become necessary if the licence is lost.
The organizers are permitted to relocate only if the licence is lost.
items.answer: Relocation could become necessary if the licence is lost.
items.explanation: Might makes the necessity expressed by have to uncertain within the stated condition.

rationales.The licence will be lost, making relocat: The if-clause does not predict loss of the licence, and might leaves the resulting necessity open.
rationales.The organizers prefer relocation if the: Have to concerns necessity rather than their preference.
rationales.The organizers are permitted to relocate: Might have to does not express permission or make licence loss the only condition for it.
rationales.Relocation could become necessary if the: Might makes the necessity expressed by have to uncertain within the stated condition.

findings: Applicant second-form sentence included a stakeholder-meeting tail and did not exclude will or must readings.
audit.microSkill: Conditional possibility of an obligation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps uncertainty about a condition separate from uncertainty about its consequences.
audit.levelReason: Two layers of unsettled information require C1 precision in interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: Conditional necessity is interpreted without predicting that the trigger will occur.

items.setupText: Choose the paraphrase that preserves this formal instruction's conditional meaning.
items.taskText: 'Should any names remain in the report, remove them before circulation.'
options: If any names remain, remove them before circulation.
Because names ought to remain, remove them before circulation.
Names are expected to remain, so remove them before circulation.
Names should have remained until circulation.
items.answer: If any names remain, remove them before circulation.
items.explanation: Initial should + subject is a formal conditional pattern meaning if this happens to be the case.

rationales.If any names remain, remove them before: Initial should + subject is a formal conditional pattern meaning if this happens to be the case.
rationales.Because names ought to remain, remove th: Conditional should does not recommend retaining names; it introduces a possible circumstance.
rationales.Names are expected to remain, so remove: The original does not predict that names will remain; it tells you what to do if they do.
rationales.Names should have remained until circula: This changes a conditional instruction into a judgment about an earlier action.

findings: Survey-report item used basic should-not selection despite C1 and mismatched its rule setup.
audit.microSkill: Inverted conditional should
audit.pedagogicalValue: Recognizes formal conditional word order without reading should as advice.
audit.levelReason: Inversion and a competing advice interpretation make a substantive C1 decision.
audit.similarityNote: Only C1 item paraphrasing a should condition without if.

items.setupText: The inspector infers that cleaning was in progress when the first visitor arrived. Choose the phrase that preserves past time, ongoing action, and the room as receiver of that action.
items.taskText: The room must ___ when the visitor arrived.
items.explanation: Must have been being cleaned combines a past inference with an ongoing passive action.

rationales.have been cleaning: This is active and makes the room do the cleaning, rather than receive it.
rationales.have been being cleaned: Must have been being cleaned combines a past inference with an ongoing passive action.
rationales.be being cleaned: This expresses an ongoing passive action but lacks the perfect form needed for the specified past inference.
rationales.have been cleaned: This suggests completed cleaning rather than cleaning still in progress at the arrival time.

findings: Reviewer appendix item allowed could, must, will, and has to under different plausible stances.
audit.microSkill: Past modal inference with continuous passive aspect
audit.pedagogicalValue: Shows how each part of a complex modal phrase contributes time, duration, or voice.
audit.levelReason: Three interacting verb-phrase choices justify C1 demand without specialist vocabulary.
audit.similarityNote: Ongoing passive cleaning extends the separate B2 progressive and passive forms.

items.setupText: The interview is over. The speaker wishes that the interviewer had not raised salary so early. Complete the retrospective preference.
items.taskText: I'd rather the interviewer ___ salary until the end.
items.explanation: Would rather + another subject + past perfect expresses a preference about an unreal alternative to a past action.

rationales.didn't mention: A past-simple clause after would rather normally expresses a present or future preference, not this earlier completed interview.
rationales.won't mention: Will not does not form the retrospective preference clause needed here.
rationales.hadn't mentioned: Would rather + another subject + past perfect expresses a preference about an unreal alternative to a past action.
rationales.hasn't mentioned: The present perfect does not express the unreal past alternative after would rather.

findings: Lena chart sentence was a noun-and-name replacement in the same elementary preference frame.
audit.microSkill: Would rather with a past-perfect subordinate clause
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes regretted past conduct from a preference about future conduct.
audit.levelReason: A completed event, changed subject, and unreal past tense create a C1 contrast.
audit.similarityNote: Retrospective other-person preference contrasts with future preference in item 2001.

items.setupText: A colleague says, 'This is her first management job.' Another replies as below. Choose the role of may in the reply.
items.taskText: 'She may be inexperienced, but she has already resolved the staffing problem.'
options: It asks whether the director is permitted to be inexperienced.
It acknowledges a drawback before introducing a counterbalancing point.
It treats the director's inexperience as an unresolved factual question.
It recommends that the director gain more experience.
items.answer: It acknowledges a drawback before introducing a counterbalancing point.
items.explanation: May ..., but ... can concede an accepted point while limiting its force with a contrasting consideration.

rationales.It asks whether the director is permitte: The statement does not request permission; it accepts a known characteristic.
rationales.It treats the director's inexperience as: The context establishes that inexperience is known; may introduces a concession here.
rationales.It recommends that the director gain mor: No recommendation is made; the speaker weighs a drawback against an achievement.
rationales.It acknowledges a drawback before introd: May ..., but ... can concede an accepted point while limiting its force with a contrasting consideration.

findings: Scholarship committee sentence repeated may well and failed to identify the intended stance.
audit.microSkill: Concessive may with a known fact
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents interpreting every may as uncertainty or permission.
audit.levelReason: Discourse context changes the modal's function, an appropriate C1 interpretive demand.
audit.similarityNote: Concedes a known drawback instead of predicting an uncertain outcome.

items.setupText: The exemption rules have not been finalized. Choose the interpretation of the layered modal phrase.
items.taskText: 'Existing members may not have to submit fresh references.'
options: Existing members will be forbidden to submit fresh references.
Existing members are certain to be exempt from providing fresh references.
Existing members will probably fail to submit required fresh references.
Existing members might be exempt from providing fresh references.
items.answer: Existing members might be exempt from providing fresh references.
items.explanation: May expresses uncertainty about the absence of a requirement: perhaps members will not have to submit references.

rationales.Existing members might be exempt from pr: May expresses uncertainty about the absence of a requirement: perhaps members will not have to submit references.
rationales.Existing members will be forbidden to su: Not applies to have to, removing necessity; it does not create a ban on submission.
rationales.Existing members are certain to be exemp: May leaves the exemption uncertain; it does not establish it as definite.
rationales.Existing members will probably fail to s: The sentence concerns whether submission is required, not whether members will comply.

findings: Applicant item recycled might have to and added an irrelevant pilot-program tail.
audit.microSkill: May not have to and the scope of negation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates uncertain exemption from prohibition and predicted non-compliance.
audit.levelReason: Negation within a phrase combining possibility and obligation suits C1.
audit.similarityNote: Possible lack of duty contrasts with possible new duty in item 2003.

items.setupText: Choose the claim made by the analyst, without strengthening it.
items.taskText: 'An increase in complaints need not indicate a decline in service quality.'
options: More complaints show that service quality has stayed the same.
Service quality is required to improve when complaints increase.
A decline in service quality makes increased complaints impossible.
More complaints do not necessarily mean that service quality has declined.
items.answer: More complaints do not necessarily mean that service quality has declined.
items.explanation: Need not can deny that an inference is necessary while leaving that inference possible.

rationales.More complaints show that service qualit: Need not rejects a necessary connection; it does not establish unchanged quality.
rationales.More complaints do not necessarily mean: Need not can deny that an inference is necessary while leaving that inference possible.
rationales.Service quality is required to improve w: This imposes a duty that the analyst's statement does not express.
rationales.A decline in service quality makes incre: This reverses the relationship and replaces lack of necessity with impossibility.

findings: Incident-report item repeated a basic should-not passive with little C1 value.
audit.microSkill: Need not denying a necessary inference
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes not necessarily from evidence of the opposite conclusion.
audit.levelReason: Assessing the strength of an analytical inference is a C1 reading skill.
audit.similarityNote: Logical necessity differs from an individual's obligation to act.

items.setupText: 'Did the reviewer read the supplementary file?' 'There's no way to tell from her comments.' A colleague then says the following. Choose its meaning.
items.taskText: 'She could have overlooked the appendix.'
options: She may actually have missed the appendix when reading.
She had an opportunity to overlook it but deliberately read it.
She ought to have ignored the appendix when reviewing the paper.
She was unable to read the appendix because access was blocked.
items.answer: She may actually have missed the appendix when reading.
items.explanation: With the event unknown, could have can speculate that overlooking it may actually have happened.

Some applicants need not attend; the others must not.
All applicants must attend, though some are exempt from attendance.
No applicant has to attend, though some may choose to.
items.answer: Some applicants must attend; others need not.
items.explanation: This assigns a requirement to one group and removes it for the other without creating a ban.

rationales.Some applicants must attend; others need: This assigns a requirement to one group and removes it for the other without creating a ban.
rationales.Some applicants need not attend; the oth: Must not prohibits the second group rather than requiring their attendance.
rationales.All applicants must attend, though some: All conflicts with the stated exemptions; the two clauses cannot preserve the policy together.
rationales.No applicant has to attend, though some: This removes the requirement from everyone, including those for whom it is compulsory.

findings: Board-objection sentence repeated routine could-have selection with an unrelated corrigendum tail.
audit.microSkill: Distributing obligation across quantified groups
audit.pedagogicalValue: Prevents a limited exemption from being rewritten as universal optionality or prohibition.
audit.levelReason: Quantifier scope and contrasting modal force must both survive the editorial rewrite.
audit.similarityNote: The requirement varies by group rather than by a future condition.

items.setupText: This invented interview protocol protects participants' choice. Choose what the nested modal phrase requires.
items.taskText: 'Participants must be allowed to decline any question.'
options: Participants must refuse questions unless the interviewer permits an answer.
Participants may refuse only when they can prove answering is impossible.
The interviewer must permit refusal; participants are not required to refuse.
The interviewer may decide whether participants are allowed to refuse.
items.answer: The interviewer must permit refusal; participants are not required to refuse.
items.explanation: Must applies to making refusal permissible. It does not impose an obligation on participants to exercise that permission.

rationales.Participants must refuse questions unles: This reverses both the protected action and the source of the requirement.
rationales.The interviewer must permit refusal; par: Must applies to making refusal permissible. It does not impose an obligation on participants to exercise that permission.
rationales.Participants may refuse only when they c: No inability condition is attached to the permission in the protocol.
rationales.The interviewer may decide whether parti: Must makes provision of that permission a duty, not a discretionary choice.

findings: Clause-interpretation item mixed a requirement setup with may and elementary malformed distractors.
audit.microSkill: Obligation to grant permission
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates who has the duty from who receives the permission.
audit.levelReason: Nested modality and different participants demand precise C2 interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: Obligation concerns permission for someone else, not their performance of an action.

items.setupText: The admissions rule is still under discussion. Choose the interpretation preserving uncertainty, requirement, and completion before applying.
items.taskText: 'Applicants may have to have completed the placement before submitting an application.'
options: Applicants probably completed the placement because they submitted applications.
A rule may require completion of the placement before an application is submitted.
Applicants are already required to finish the placement after applying.
Applicants are allowed to submit an application without completing the placement.
items.answer: A rule may require completion of the placement before an application is submitted.
items.explanation: May marks an uncertain requirement; have to expresses that requirement; have completed locates completion before applying.

rationales.Applicants probably completed the placem: This turns an uncertain rule into an inference about actual applicants; the sentence establishes neither event.
rationales.Applicants are already required to finis: May leaves the rule unsettled, and before places completion earlier than submission.
rationales.A rule may require completion of the pla: May marks an uncertain requirement; have to expresses that requirement; have completed locates completion before applying.
rationales.Applicants are allowed to submit an appl: The phrase considers a possible completion requirement rather than granting an exemption.

findings: Dissent item reused a counterfactual frame and an incoherent counterargument-table tail.
audit.microSkill: Possible obligation concerning prior completion
audit.pedagogicalValue: Assigns a separate function to each layer of a long modal phrase.
audit.levelReason: Uncertainty, necessity, and relative completion time interact in a C2 parsing task.
audit.similarityNote: Three modal/time layers go beyond the single inferred past duty at C1.

items.setupText: A critic ends a review with this sentence. Choose the recommendation it conveys.
items.taskText: 'I cannot recommend this performance too highly.'
options: The critic gives the performance an exceptionally strong recommendation.
The critic recommends it, but only with substantial reservations.
The critic cannot judge the performance because evidence is missing.
The critic advises readers against attending the performance.
items.answer: The critic gives the performance an exceptionally strong recommendation.
items.explanation: Cannot ... too highly means that even very high praise would not be excessive, so the recommendation is emphatic.

rationales.The critic recommends it, but only with: The too highly idiom intensifies the recommendation here rather than limiting it.
rationales.The critic cannot judge the performance: In cannot recommend too highly, the negative intensifies the recommendation; it does not signal a lack of evidence.
rationales.The critic advises readers against atten: This mistakes the negative wording for a negative recommendation; the idiom has positive force.
rationales.The critic gives the performance an exce: Cannot ... too highly means that even very high praise would not be excessive, so the recommendation is emphatic.

findings: Agency disclosure item repeated ordinary should-not-have criticism with generic messages.
audit.microSkill: Emphatic praise through cannot ... too highly
audit.pedagogicalValue: Resolves the apparent negative against the construction's positive pragmatic force.
audit.levelReason: An idiomatic scope reversal must be interpreted in a stated evaluative context.
audit.similarityNote: An apparent negative intensifies praise rather than drawing an evidential conclusion.

items.setupText: After the team agrees on a spending limit, a colleague selects the premium option. Read the response below with stress on WOULD. Choose its implication.
items.taskText: 'You WOULD choose the one option that exceeds the budget.'
options: The speaker is unsure whether the colleague has made any choice yet.
The choice is presented as irritatingly typical of the colleague.
The speaker is offering permission to exceed the budget next time.
The colleague would choose that option only if an unstated condition occurred.
items.answer: The choice is presented as irritatingly typical of the colleague.
items.explanation: Stressed would can react to a known event as characteristic and exasperating; it need not place the event in an unreal condition.

rationales.The choice is presented as irritatingly: Stressed would can react to a known event as characteristic and exasperating; it need not place the event in an unreal condition.
rationales.The speaker is unsure whether the collea: The context establishes that the choice has just been made.
rationales.The speaker is offering permission to ex: The comment criticizes a known choice rather than granting future permission.
rationales.The colleague would choose that option o: The utterance reacts to an actual choice; its force is characteristic disapproval, not an incomplete hypothetical result.

findings: Luis submission item was another name-only should-have duplicate, too elementary for C2.
audit.microSkill: Reactive stressed would as characteristic disapproval
audit.pedagogicalValue: Uses actual occurrence and tone to distinguish an evaluative would from counterfactual grammar.
audit.levelReason: Recovering an interpersonal implication from stress and factual context is a C2 pragmatic task.
audit.similarityNote: Reactive would comments on a completed event, unlike C1's persistent present will.

items.setupText: A says, 'I know the client asked us to wait until tomorrow, but I'm calling him tonight.' B replies as below. Choose the interpretation best supported by their exchange.
items.taskText: 'If you must call tonight, at least keep it brief.'
options: B recognizes an external obligation to make the call tonight.
B authorizes the call because A has satisfied a stated condition.
B yields to A's insistence but asks A to limit the disruption.
B doubts that A intends to call and challenges the claim.
items.answer: B yields to A's insistence but asks A to limit the disruption.
items.explanation: A insists despite the client's request to wait. If you must accommodates that insistence; at least keep it brief limits the action rather than endorsing it.

rationales.B recognizes an external obligation to m: The only external request is to wait until tomorrow. The pressure to call tonight comes from A's insistence.
rationales.B yields to A's insistence but asks A to: A insists despite the client's request to wait. If you must accommodates that insistence; at least keep it brief limits the action rather than endorsing it.
rationales.B authorizes the call because A has sati: No permission condition has been met. B responds to A's determination and adds a request about how the call is handled.
rationales.B doubts that A intends to call and chal: Keep it brief treats the intended call as something to manage; B does not challenge whether A intends to make it.

findings: Board-objection sentence recycled could-have with an expert-testimony tail and non-specific feedback.
audit.microSkill: Reluctant concession with if you must
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes echoing an interlocutor's insistence from endorsing a necessity.
audit.levelReason: The modal's interpersonal source and the limiting follow-up require C2 pragmatic interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: Concedes a person's insistence rather than conceding a factual premise.

items.setupText: After checking the attendance record, the secretary makes the remark below. Choose the role of should have in that remark.
items.taskText: 'It is extraordinary that the chair should have missed the one briefing devoted to this issue.'
options: It presents an established event as striking or surprising.
It identifies missing the briefing as the chair's unfulfilled duty.
It leaves open whether the chair missed the briefing at all.
It predicts a missed briefing later than the present discussion.
items.answer: It presents an established event as striking or surprising.
items.explanation: After an evaluative expression such as it is extraordinary, should can highlight a reaction to a fact without expressing obligation.

rationales.It identifies missing the briefing as th: The sentence treats missing it as an established event, not as an action the chair ought to have performed.
rationales.It leaves open whether the chair missed: The context establishes the absence; should is evaluative here rather than a marker of factual uncertainty.
rationales.It presents an established event as stri: After an evaluative expression such as it is extraordinary, should can highlight a reaction to a fact without expressing obligation.
rationales.It predicts a missed briefing later than: Should have missed refers to the completed event under evaluation, not a later briefing.

findings: Clause item repeated elementary may selection and attached an unrelated compliance-addendum phrase.
audit.microSkill: Evaluative should have with an established fact
audit.pedagogicalValue: Separates emotional evaluation from obligation, uncertainty, and prediction.
audit.levelReason: The learner must interpret a marked formal construction without its familiar normative reading.
audit.similarityNote: Factual surprise contrasts with tentative conditional should in item 2026.

items.setupText: A supplier says, 'We'll bill your firm for correcting the error in our installation.' The customer replies as below. Choose the force of the question.
items.taskText: 'Why should we have to pay to correct their mistake?'
options: It asks how the payment can be processed efficiently.
It expresses doubt about whether the supplier made any mistake.
It concludes that the speaker's group already paid the charge.
It challenges why this group should bear the cost.
items.answer: It challenges why this group should bear the cost.
items.explanation: Rhetorical why should challenges justification; have to identifies the obligation being challenged.

rationales.It asks how the payment can be processed: The question challenges who should bear the duty rather than how payment works.
rationales.It expresses doubt about whether the sup: Their mistake is treated as the basis of the objection, not an uncertain event.
rationales.It concludes that the speaker's group al: Have to pay describes a requirement, not a completed payment.
rationales.It challenges why this group should bear: Rhetorical why should challenges justification; have to identifies the obligation being challenged.

findings: Dissent item reused a simple counterfactual and appended a temporally inconsistent model-revision tail.
audit.microSkill: Rhetorical should questioning the justification of an obligation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Distinguishes requesting a reason from rejecting the premise that a duty is fair.
audit.levelReason: Interpreting a rhetorical question with nested obligation requires C2 pragmatic precision.
audit.similarityNote: Challenges an obligation's legitimacy instead of denying that the obligation exists.

items.setupText: During discussion of a proposed compulsory evening timetable, the manager says the following to an employee. Choose the interpretation of the preference.
items.taskText: 'I'd rather you didn't have to attend every evening session.'
options: The manager prefers the employee to be free of the requirement to attend them all.
The manager prefers the employee to be prohibited from attending any evening session.
The manager states that the employee has already missed all evening sessions.
The manager prefers compulsory attendance at fewer sessions but rules out voluntary attendance at others.
items.answer: The manager prefers the employee to be free of the requirement to attend them all.
items.explanation: Would rather introduces a preference; didn't have to removes the duty, not the option of attending voluntarily.

rationales.The manager prefers the employee to be f: Would rather introduces a preference; didn't have to removes the duty, not the option of attending voluntarily.
rationales.The manager prefers the employee to be p: Absence of obligation does not create a prohibition, and every is not equivalent to any in this rewrite.
rationales.The manager states that the employee has: The past form after would rather expresses a current preference, not a report of past absence.
rationales.The manager prefers compulsory attendanc: The sentence does not impose a new smaller quota or rule out additional voluntary attendance.

findings: Final agency disclosure item repeated should-not-have criticism and added an awkward ruling-time tail.
audit.microSkill: Preference over absence of a quantified obligation
audit.pedagogicalValue: Keeps preference, negation, necessity, and the range of sessions separate.
audit.levelReason: Multiple interacting scopes and a non-past preference form make a substantive C2 interpretation.
audit.similarityNote: A preference concerns freedom from duty, not the preferred performance or non-performance itself.
